en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Song of Vessantara [Ka].
Endowed with the thirty-two marks,
you gave excellent gifts while giving;
thus you attained the state of Vessantara.
Wandering through the ocean of existence.
[Kha] Wandering from pair to pair,
Janānanda and Yasodhīra fell into intoxication;
you too have fallen into it in this ocean of existence.
[Ga] Now I shall tell you,
O Nandinī, of my birth there.
"O wise ones, grant me the opportunity;
even you poets should rejoice!
Ninety-one eons ago..."
The Leader named Vipassī,
the possessor of vision, has arisen in the world to deliver his disciples to safety.
The Fully Enlightened One was staying at the delightful Khemārāma in the Migadāya park,
near Bandhumatī.
He then dwelt in that city.
In that city of Bandhumā, he ruled his kingdom with righteousness.
That king had two daughters,
beautiful in all their limbs; indeed,
each was a king among women.
He presented to Bandhumā a golden garland worth a thousand [pieces of gold] and sandalwood that was beyond price.
King Bandhumāra gave sandalwood to his eldest daughter,
and a golden garland to his youngest.
Having learned of this from their daughter,
both of them thought:
"There is not even a little remaining of that."
We honor the Fortunate One with a mind full of serene confidence. Then,
sandalwood powder—
Having had it built,

Having scattered the remaining sandalwood in the hut while it was still fragrant,
he made this aspiration:
May I become the Mother of the Buddha.
Having caused a golden garland and a breast-covering to be made as an act of serene faith;
The youngest sisters, with limbs the color of gold,
made offerings to the Blessed One;
in this way, they also made their aspiration.
May this clarity of mine remain unshakable within my body as I wander from existence to existence.
Both of them, being royal maidens,
remained as long as their life-span lasted and were reborn in the highest heaven.
Experiencing both joy and sorrow,
they wandered through the worlds of humans and devas,
encountering both happiness and pain.
For ninety-one eons,
having been liberated from the suffering of hell, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, they were among those [in the human realm].
The youngest daughter of King Kiki, named Urañchadā, having lived her life,
has attained final nibbāna.
But there, among the daughters of King Kiki, she was the eldest,
named Dhammā, who had been well-disciplined.
A celibate student from her youth,
having passed away from there, O Deva,
she was born again and again among humans.
Once, while wandering, you were the chief queen of Pūrindada,
anointed with red sandalwood paste.
Limpitā was the name of her body;
through the excellence of her performed merit,
she was called Phussatī by name.
The Lord of Devas, having perceived that the goddess’s life-span was exhausted, like one whose time has run out,
[approached] that goddess with his retinue.
The descendant of Māgha, having placed the joy of the Nesas upon the back of his own couch,
covered him with a great [blanket].
Standing by his bedside,
he said this to Phussati:
"I shall grant you ten boons."
O Phussatā of excellent complexion;
whatever boon you desire to obtain,
I shall surely cause you to receive that boon.
Having heard this, Queen Phussatī,
her hair standing on end with horror, did not realize that ten thousand [beings] had been destroyed.
He said this to himself:
"O Lord of Devas, you have committed a wicked deed against me,
one that is most unpleasant."
"O Rambhā, desiring my death,
they surely think such things;
O noble lady, no evil has been committed."
Do not come back to me as one who is unloved;
your merit has been completely exhausted,
therefore I speak thus to you.
Death will come to you in my presence;
there will be separation from me.
Accept these [offerings] from me.
While Vāmadeva was speaking,
having heard the words of Sakka and knowing his own mortality, he said:
Desiring to obtain Varesā, she spoke thus to the Lord of Devas:

In the palace of King Sivi,
there was a chief queen named Phussatī,
blue-eyed like a doe.
May I obtain a horse with a dark-blue face;
may they carry me, who am pregnant with an excellent son, as I make this request.
The middle part is not elevated.
May palitā flowers and alambā flowers grow there.
Dust shall not soil your body,
and you shall be released even from what is blameworthy.
Whatever boon was requested, O auspicious lady—
By me, through my ascetic power,
this has been given to you with a joyful heart;
you shall obtain all human desires.
Then, having emerged from that womb,

such was the conception of the Great Queen.
By the power of King Madda.

Beneath a white umbrella,
she gave birth to a woman of most excellent form,
who was anointed with red sandalwood paste.
She too was embodied in that very same way; therefore,
the brahmins gave her the name Phussatī.
Having performed the auspicious rites and others,
mounted upon the palanquin,
with great ceremony, he departed.
Noble women stood there,
endowed with sweet milk, possessing smooth,
full breasts, and in the bloom of youth.
The nurses of the Kṣatriya women gave them milk for their sustenance;
they grew like those whose hopes have been fulfilled.
From lap to lap and hand to hand,
the dancing girls and the royal maidens delighted him with their songs and dances.
In the form of a celestial nymph,
sixteen years of age,
she carried away the essence of his eyes.
Then, while passing through the kingdom of Sivi,
King Sivi established his sovereignty there at Jetuttara.
His son was named Kāresi-siñca,
who possessed great renown;
having reached maturity, he was handsome.
Like a celestial youth, you are full-bodied;
in both height and girth,
you are skilled in various archery techniques.
While still alive, he bestowed his own kingdom upon his son Siñcaya,
so that the king might see it.
Having brought the highly precious Phussatī,

She was the chief queen among sixteen thousand women; she was Phussatī,
the foremost of them all.
Beholding one another with eyes full of affection,
they spoke kindly to each other.
Then the Lord of Devas thought:

The hero does not achieve success.

in the abode of the ten-fold [powers].
Having passed away from that state,

having gone to Brahmā, the thousand-eyed one spoke this to him.

They were born separately.
When the Great Being had entered her womb,
the queen became like a lotus-pond.
Desiring to give a great gift,
she distributed much wealth at the gate of the royal palace.
And in the middle of the city,
at each of the four gates, alms-halls were established and filled with gifts to be given.
Having had six hundred thousand [images] made,
he bestowed them all day after day upon everyone.
Desiring to give a gift, the king,
having summoned the brahmins, explained the reason for his departure.
The reciter of omens was asked, "What will happen?
so that it might be known. [He replied:

When the queen’s womb was filled,
at the gift of the Hehita-biratodāna,
the brahmins spoke thus.
Having heard the words of the brahmins,
the lord of men, with a joyful mind,
gave the gift of the six gifts.
The halls were well-furnished.
From the moment of taking rebirth,
the Bodhisatta was conscious.
Like the surge of a new ocean from its starting point,
a vast and abundant gain arose;
they sent forth a gift of honor.
In the realm of King Jambumaṇḍala,
through the power of the Bodhisatta,
various kshatriyas from many countries [gathered].
He spoke the rebuttal to the Great Seer regarding rebirth;
he caused the King to dwell in royal happiness.
They did whatever they desired.
By the power of the Buddha-seed,
the people were filled with joy.
In that time of rain, the clouds poured forth;
it was a season of abundant food.
Together with her son, under the full moon, she went.
While his mother was playing,
a great and vast delight arose there for all the people.
While the Queen was carrying the embryo,
when ten months were fulfilled,
she desired to see the city.
Then they reported this to the King.
Having said, "Excellent, Bhaddā!",
he [entered] the city as a god enters his own city.
The king had it adorned as an increase of joy for the queen; then,
having caused the queen to mount [the elephant], he—
He had a magnificent, auspicious chariot made,
and he caused the entire city to be decorated.
In the midst of the street of the Vessas,
the winds born of karma caused the proper and improper places,
and the paths and non-paths, to tremble.
While the queen was still on her way,
the ministers quickly informed the king of her departure.
He had a beautiful house built;
he lived in that street. While she was staying there, just as she was dwelling there...
Vijayī, free from fear from any quarter,
gave birth to a son who was stainless,
perfectly pure, and resembled a mass of gold.
Having closed his eyes,
he emerged from his mother’s womb with a serene and pleasing appearance.
He looked at his mother’s face:
“Mother, I shall give a gift;
do you have any wealth?”
Stretching out his neck,
he spoke thus repeatedly;
hearing this, his mother rejoiced.
"Give me whatever I desire as a gift.
"Father," he said, and thereupon he gave him a purse containing a thousand [pieces].
In his births as Mahosadha, Vessantara, and Mahāsiddhattha,
he spoke to his mother regarding the Bodhi tree.
Attached to the moments of birth and so forth,
people rejoiced upon seeing wonders and marvels,
even when merely hearing of them.
Clapping their hands and laughing,
they raised a shout of victory;
they called out, "Vessantara!"
The naming ceremony was an auspicious occasion;
he was designated as a Brāhmaṇa because he was born in the Vessavīthi street.
On the day after giving birth, she,
wandering alone through the sky,
[beheld] that all-white elephant together with her female companions.
By the power of the Bodhisatta, he brought one elephant keeper who was considered auspicious.
Having left it there,
he departed from the elephant stable with great care,
for the sake of the Great Being who had been born there.
Having established the condition for that,
the people known as the Nāgas acted together in unison as a condition.

The Mahāsattasaja Jātaka:

you sprinkled [the water].

Bhiru, Pāyāsi, and Yobbañña;

Of sixty thousand [disciples],

so too did sixty thousand youths of great renown.
The Bodhisatta was raised with a great retinue;

Having had him adorned with beautiful,
well-fastened ornaments, he caused his own son, who delights in giving, to be arrayed in splendor.
Having released him from the nurses,
that great being, at the age of four or five years, gave him away.

The giver of nurses, Nanda,

was beloved by the Omniscient One.
In this very manner,
nine times the young maidservant adorned herself with ornaments for the nurses.
With no protector and no refuge,
the wise one thought thus during his eighth year:
Seated upon a couch of glory in a circular palace,
he gave a gift as if it were an external offering.
My mind is not yet fully satisfied;
for I am giving away my internal [belongings] as if they were external.
If anyone were to ask me for my head,
adorned with its jeweled crest,
I would cut it off and give it to him.
With a dejected mind, he would have approached me and entreated my heart,
having pierced his chest with a sword.
Having removed that [impurity] from him,
I would give it to him with a joyful mind;
even if he were to ask for my eyes, I would give them.
Having torn them out right now with a blade, I would give them to him,
even though they are dripping with blood.
If one should ask me for my hands, feet, or ears,
I would cut them off and give them away.
To fulfill his wish,
someone might quickly cut flesh from every part of my body.
Having cut it into pieces,
he would give me flesh along with blood,
thinking, "May I become his slave."
If anyone there should speak thus:
"Having summoned my own mother,
I shall give even myself."
As he was reflecting thus,
the great earth trembled;
this [earth] roared on all sides.
In the Kuñjara forest,
King Meru bowed down toward him,
facing Jetuttara as if before his very eyes.
At that moment, he stood in the city like a young bamboo-shoot trembling from the fear of a great roar.
Then he rained down like a cloud,
thundering in every direction with a great torrent of thick rain.
Many flashes of lightning issued forth from the creeper on all sides,
and rainbows appeared.
Then there was a falling of meteors;
right there, the King, the Lord of the Devas,
being delighted, clapped his hands.
"Excellent, excellent!
cried Mahābrahmā, filled with joy;
he then departed from the Brahma-world.
The earth’s surface became like a mandala;
it was a marvel, a wonder,
a great and singular clamor.
Thus, having produced many beings,

Sixteen years old,

Shining then with beauty and youth like a blossoming *sāla* tree,
he was as if desirous of giving to him.

She who always follows behind,
the goddess who acts agreeably,

A hundred thousand sixteen thousand women,

instrumental music, and song.

Distributing day after day,

To that web-weaving spider, a daughter was born,

With a great retinue,

Falling asleep to song and dance,

Six times he gazed from his position atop the back of a magnificent,

the entire kingdom of Kaliṅga—
Oppressed by the fear of famine,

The merchants, all the country folk,

Driven by the fear of famine, the king,

In the kingdom of Meghaṃkaliṅka,

O Great King, desiring a time of abundant food for the peaceful kingdom,

The son of Siñcayā, born of the great Vessantara lineage of Jetuttara,

The elephant Kiramaṅgala-kuñjara;

Mahāmegha, Osadhi, and Vijju;

the king, like a royal swan,
assembled the brahmins in the royal courtyard.

"Bring the noble elephant to the presence of Vessantara,

Having gone and made this request,

The brahmins [spoke] to the eight kings.

they went to the elephant Jetuttara to lead away that one who was beautiful in every limb.
Traveling by stages,
those brahmins reached Jetuttara while enjoying their meal.
They stayed in the halls of charity.

intending to beg for alms.
The supreme kings of the mind,
awaiting his arrival,
waited there with great devotion.
When the tip of the alms-food was being smeared with ghee, O Asura, together with your retinue,

Adorned with ornaments,

The king, having looked upon the great assembly at the eastern gate,
[addressed] the great assembly.
Terrified and with agitated minds,
the brahmins there could not find any space to make their request.
Having moved from there to the southern gate,
they proceeded to the exalted region where the supreme king resided.

having looked toward the eastern gate at the gift pavilion, they remained.
The king, mounted upon the neck of an elephant,
went as far as the gateway.
Seeing that the king had arrived, he [stood there].

the king and his retinue, including the brahmins,
[give] the elephant to them and the place where it stood.
With a mind full of generosity,

which were previously unheard, heart-stirring,
and like a right-spiraling conch upon a mountain.
"Stretching out their right arms,
standing before me,
what do these brahmins ask of me?"

Having heard this regarding the elephant that is entirely white,
one should not grieve even for what is internal.
"I desire this now;
they are begging from me for external things.

Fulfilling the desires of those who entreated him,
thus did he of radiant splendor speak while seated upon the back of an elephant.
I do not waver from what I have given away,
even when Brahmins beg from me—
be it as white as Mount Kelāsa.

banish him from the kingdom to the forest.

Vessantara’s residence. There,
